slides.title: The whole machine on one screen
slides.summary: Putting it all together: an LLM reads some text and guesses what comes next. That is all it does.
body: You've now met every part: tokens, embeddings, attention, the MLP and the output. Here they are together on one screen, and next, how they actually run on a GPU.
An LLM does one simple job: it reads some text and guesses the next word.
Give it “The cat sat on the”. It gives every possible next word a score: “mat” scores high, “moon” scores low.
<mark>To write a full answer, it repeats that job: guess one word, add it to the text, guess again.</mark> The next slide shows this loop.

Each stage on the right turns one block of numbers into another. A block of numbers with several dimensions is called a tensor, and its shape lists how big each dimension is. Following the shapes is the quickest way to understand how the model works. Four letters come up everywhere:

ul: B, batch size: how many separate texts are handled at once.
n, sequence length: how many tokens are in each text.
d, model width: how many numbers describe each token. Usually 4,096 or more.
V, vocabulary size: how many different tokens the model knows. Often 100,000 or more.

body: Click a stage on the right to jump to its chapter.

viz.html: Typical sizes: d = 4,096, N = 32 layers, V = 128,000. When generating, only the scores for the last token matter.

figure.alt: Text is split into token IDs, each ID becomes a vector of d numbers, the vectors flow through N transformer blocks, and the final layer gives a score for every vocabulary token. Softmax turns the last position's scores into probabilities, one token is picked, appended to the text, and the whole pass runs again.
figure.caption: The whole model on one page. Follow the shapes: [n] → [n, d] → [n, V]. Numbers are illustrative.

slides.title: The loop, in two stages
slides.summary: You've seen the loop: one token per run, fed back in. On real hardware it has two very different stages, prefill and decode.
body: A quick recap from Transformer architecture: the model writes one token per run, adds it to the text and runs again, until the end token wins. This is autoregressive decoding. Press Run one step to watch it.

ul: Prefill: the whole prompt is processed in one go, all its tokens together. You see it as the short pause before the first word: the time to first token.
Decode: then one token per run, each waiting for the one before. You see it as the steady word-by-word typing.

body: <mark>The two stages use the GPU in completely different ways.</mark> The next two slides show where everything lives on a GPU, and why prefill keeps it busy while decode mostly waits.

steps.caption: Just the prompt. Step 1 processes all 3 tokens at once (prefill).
Run 2 done. The text is now 4 tokens long; the model reads it all again (or reuses its cache).
Run 3 done. The text is now 5 tokens long; the model reads it all again (or reuses its cache).
Run 4 done. The text is now 6 tokens long; the model reads it all again (or reuses its cache).
Run 5 done. The text is now 7 tokens long; the model reads it all again (or reuses its cache).
Run 6 done. The text is now 8 tokens long; the model reads it all again (or reuses its cache).
Run 7 done. The text is now 9 tokens long; the model reads it all again (or reuses its cache).
Run 8 done. The text is now 10 tokens long; the model reads it all again (or reuses its cache).
It wrote the end token <eos>, so it stops.

slides.title: Inside a GPU: where the maths happens
slides.summary: A GPU keeps the model's weights in its own memory and does the maths in thousands of cores on its chip. The weights stream between the two, a tile at a time.
body: The model runs on GPUs, inside a server in a data centre. The server also has a CPU, main memory and a disk, but they only run the program and store files. The model's maths happens on the GPUs.

ul: GPU memory: 80 GB on an NVIDIA H100. This is where the weights live. Llama 3 8B takes about 16 GB; it's copied in once and stays there.

Compute cores, on the GPU's main chip: thousands of small calculators working side by side, about 1,000 trillion calculations a second. They can only work on numbers in the tiny on-chip memory next to them: on an H100, a 50 MB cache plus small scratch areas by each group of cores, tens of megabytes in total.
The link between memory and chip: about 3.3 TB a second.

body.note: Think of a factory. GPU memory is the warehouse, the link is the conveyor belt, and the cores are very fast workers.

body.h: How the weights reach the cores

ul: The model runs layer by layer. One layer of Llama 3 8B holds about 218 million weights (its attention and MLP tables), about 436 MB. Not even one layer fits on the chip.

So each weight table is cut into tiles, often 128 × 64 numbers. A tile is copied across the link into on-chip memory, used by the cores, then overwritten by the next one: tile after tile, table after table, layer after layer.

body: <mark>Every run through the model streams all 16 GB of weights across the link, one tile at a time.</mark>

body.more: Why not keep all the weights on the chip?
text: On-chip memory (SRAM) needs about 6 transistors per bit, built on the main chip, the most expensive silicon there is. GPU memory (HBM) stores a bit with 1 transistor and a tiny capacitor, in stacks beside the chip. That's why the chip holds tens of megabytes and GPU memory holds 80 GB.

Every computer has the same ladder: registers, on-chip cache, GPU or main memory, then disk. Each step is bigger, but slower and further from the cores. Memory can be big, or fast and close, but not both.

A few companies take the other path. Groq and Cerebras build chips with far more on-chip memory and keep the weights there. Decode is very fast, but a big model needs hundreds of Groq chips, or Cerebras's chip the size of a whole silicon wafer.

body: <mark>For any job, ask one question: are the cores busy calculating, or waiting for the next tile to arrive?</mark> The next slide answers it for prefill and decode.

figure.alt: One GPU inside a server, running Llama 3 8B on an NVIDIA H100; numbers are approximate. Left, a server: a CPU that runs the program, main memory as a loading area, a disk that stores files, and 8 GPUs. One GPU is enlarged on the right. It has three parts. First, GPU memory, 80 GB, where the weights live: Llama 3 8B takes 16 GB, the rest is free space. This is the warehouse. Second, the link from GPU memory to the chip, about 3.3 terabytes per second; weights stream across it every time they are used. This is the conveyor belt. Third, the GPU chip itself: a tiny on-chip memory of a few tens of megabytes, and thousands of compute cores doing about 1,000 trillion calculations a second. These are the workers. Below left, how the weights reach the cores: one layer, about 436 MB, is cut into tiles of about 128 by 64 numbers; each tile is copied into on-chip memory one at a time, used by the cores, then replaced by the next, so each run streams all 16 GB across the link. Below right, why the weights are not kept on the chip: on-chip memory (SRAM) needs 6 transistors per bit on costly chip area, so it holds tens of megabytes and is very fast; GPU memory (HBM) needs 1 transistor and 1 capacitor per bit, stacked beside the chip, so it holds 80 GB but is slower to reach.
figure.caption: One GPU: weights in memory, maths in the cores, and tiles of weights streaming across the link between them.

slides.title: Prefill and decode, step by step
slides.summary: Prefill multiplies a whole table of prompt tokens by each tile of weights; decode multiplies a single row. Same weights, very different use of the GPU.
body: Each token is a vector of 4,096 numbers. 4,096 is the model's dimension: how many numbers it uses to describe each token.

body.h: Prefill: the whole prompt at once

ul: All the prompt tokens are already known, so nothing has to wait. Say there are 1,000: they're stacked into one table, 1,000 × 4,096.
In each layer, that table is multiplied by each weight table, for example the 4,096 × 4,096 one that makes the queries. One big multiplication, not 1,000 small ones.

The work is cut into tiles, and every group of cores takes some at the same time. The result, again 1,000 × 4,096, goes on to the next layer, 32 times in all. Attention works the same way, since every earlier token is already there.

Each tile of weights crosses the link once and is used 1,000 times while it's on the chip, so the cores never wait. The limit is how fast they calculate: compute-bound. That's about 16 trillion calculations, at least 16 ms: the time to first token.

body.h: Decode: one token at a time

ul: Token 1,001 isn't known until it's predicted, and token 1,002 depends on it. So each step has just one new token: a table 1 × 4,096.
The same weight tables are used, and the work is still shared across the cores, but each gets only a sliver: one row instead of 1,000. Most of the calculating power goes unused.

Yet every tile of weights must still cross the link: all 16 GB, for one token. The maths takes about 0.02 ms; reading takes about 5 ms. The limit is memory speed: memory-bound, at most about 200 tokens a second.

body: <mark>Prefill uses each tile of weights 1,000 times; decode uses it once. That single difference makes prefill compute-bound and decode memory-bound.</mark>
Servers fight decode's waste by batching: answering many people at once, so each tile does work for many tokens per trip. The KV cache (see Output & inference) saves redoing earlier tokens.

figure.alt: Prefill and decode, step by step, for one layer's query table in Llama 3 8B, whose dimension is 4,096. Top, prefill: the whole prompt of 1,000 tokens is a table of 1,000 by 4,096, multiplied by the 4,096 by 4,096 query weights to give a result of 1,000 by 4,096, cut into tiles. All compute cores are lit. Each tile of weights crosses the link once and is then used 1,000 times on the chip, and every group of cores works at the same time. It is compute-bound: the cores never wait; about 16 trillion calculations, at least 16 milliseconds, the time to first token. Bottom, decode: one new token is a single row, 1 by 4,096, times the same 4,096 by 4,096 weights, giving a single row. The cores are only dimly lit. Every tile still crosses the link, all 16 GB, used for just 1 token; each core gets a sliver of work, 1 row instead of 1,000. It is memory-bound: the cores mostly wait, about 0.02 milliseconds of maths against about 5 milliseconds of reading, at most about 200 tokens a second.
figure.caption: The same weight tiles: used 1,000 times per trip in prefill, once per trip in decode.

slides.title: Batching and the KV cache
slides.summary: An inference server keeps one copy of the weights and one KV cache per conversation, and puts one row per person into every decode step. Rows never mix, and attention reads only each person's own cache.
body: Decode leaves most of the GPU waiting (previous slide). Inference servers fix that with two tools: the KV cache and batching, answering many people at once.

ul: Attention compares each new token's query with the keys of every earlier token, and blends their values. Without a cache, every step would recompute all of them: step 1,000 would redo 1,000 tokens.

So each token's key and value are saved, in every layer, the first time they're worked out. Prefill writes the whole prompt's; each decode step adds one token's; when the answer ends, the cache is freed.
Size, for Llama 3 8B: 2 (key and value) × 32 layers × 8 head groups × 128 numbers × 2 bytes ≈ 128 KB per token. 1,000 tokens ≈ 128 MB; a full 128,000-token context ≈ 16 GB, as much as the model.
GPU memory holds one copy of the weights, shared by everyone, and one KV cache per conversation. After 16 GB of weights, an 80 GB GPU has room for roughly half a million tokens of cache.
Each decode step stacks the newest token of every conversation into one table, one row per person (64 people: 64 × 4,096). Each tile of weights crosses the link once and does work for all 64 rows.
Rows never mix. In a matrix multiplication, each row of the result comes only from the same row of the input, so Ana's row gives Ana's result.
Attention reads only each row's own cache. The server hands every row its own conversation's keys and values, so conversations of different lengths sit side by side.

body: <mark>One copy of the weights, one cache per conversation, one row per person: rows share the weights but never each other's numbers.</mark>

ul: PagedAttention (vLLM) stores caches in small blocks, say 16 tokens each. Each conversation has a block table listing its blocks; a growing conversation gets a new block, and a finished one frees its blocks.
Continuous batching: the batch changes every step. Finished answers leave at once; new prompts are prefilled and join the next step, so nobody waits for the slowest answer.

Throughput vs latency: bigger batches give more tokens per second in total, but every cache needs memory, every step reads every cache (64 people × 1,000 tokens = 8 GB, on top of the weights), and very large batches make the cores busy again, so each person's tokens arrive a little slower. Servers pick a balance.

body: <mark class="info">The one exception to keeping caches apart: when requests start with exactly the same text, like an app's system prompt, that part's cache can be shared, because identical text gives identical keys and values.</mark>

figure.alt: Batching and the KV cache on one GPU running Llama 3 8B for three people, Ana, Ben and Kai. Left, GPU memory of 80 GB: one copy of the 16 GB weights, shared by everyone, then a separate KV cache for each person, of different lengths, and free space with room for about 500,000 tokens of cache, at about 128 KB per token. Middle, one decode step: the newest token of each conversation is stacked into a batch table, one row per person, 64 by 4,096; it is multiplied by a tile of weights that crosses the link once, giving 64 results; row 1 of the result comes only from row 1 of the input. Right, attention: each person's query reads only that person's own cache, at token 50, token 3,000 and token 900; an arrow from Ana's query to Ben's cache is crossed out, because a row never reads another conversation's cache. Bottom, continuous batching over nine steps: Ana and Kai continue every step; Ben's answer ends at step 4 and Ben leaves; a new request is prefilled at step 6 and joins from step 7. PagedAttention keeps each cache in 16-token blocks with one block table per conversation, and identical starting text such as a shared system prompt can share its blocks.
figure.caption: One copy of the weights, one cache per conversation, and one row per person in every step.

slides.title: A short glossary
slides.summary: The few words that come up on almost every slide.
body: Each term is explained fully the first time it matters. Come back to this list if a word on a later slide feels unfamiliar.
Two ideas matter more than any single definition:

ul: Everything is numbers. Text becomes whole numbers, those become vectors, and the model just does maths on the vectors.

Behaviour comes from learned numbers. Nobody writes an LLM's knowledge or style by hand. Billions of numbers are adjusted during training until the model predicts text well, and everything it can do comes from those numbers.

body.note: A handy comparison with software: training is like a very long, very expensive build that produces a file (the weights). Inference is running that file. Most of this course is about inference; the Training chapter covers the build.

items.label: Token
items.sub: A piece of text: a word, part of a word, or a symbol.

items.label: Vocabulary
items.sub: The fixed list of every token the model knows, each with a number as its ID.

items.label: Vector / tensor
items.sub: A list of numbers / a block of numbers with several dimensions.

items.label: Embedding
items.sub: The vector that represents one token inside the model.

items.label: Parameter (weight)
items.sub: One learned number inside the model. Model sizes count these.

items.label: Layer (block)
items.sub: One repeated unit of the model: attention, then an MLP (a small neural network).

items.label: Forward pass
items.sub: One run of the model, from token IDs in to scores out.

items.label: Logit
items.sub: The raw score the model gives each possible next token.

items.label: Softmax
items.sub: Turns a list of scores into probabilities that add up to 1.

items.label: Hallucination
items.sub: Fluent, confident text that isn't true.

items.label: Training / inference
items.sub: Learning the parameters / using them to generate text.
